cells.tense: The pen is in your hand and you are choosing what gets felt through.
cells.ask: Take the pull you already trust and give it more time than is practical today. Let it grow into something you can point at before you sort anything else.
cells.core:
You can tell which pulls are worth your attention before you can argue for them. Not the loudest thing wanting an answer, and not the urgent one — the one that keeps its weight when nothing is pressing on you. You keep feeding that one your time, so it fattens into something you can feel, and the feeling settles into a satisfaction that doesn't need defending.

That is the balance: picking and feeling running together, so what you imagine actually arrives somewhere. What it costs to keep is saying plainly what you're attending to. Tell someone who knows this life what you're feeding and why. You won't have to argue for it — you'll just be reporting.
cells.sheetLine: You can tell what's worth your attention, and you keep feeding it.

cells.tense: You are bracing at a future that cannot be written in, so you grip every pull that might pay off.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're looking after and give it a month of ordinary, bounded care. No pushing, no checking it daily. Stop when the month ends.
cells.core:
You are handling too many pulls at once. Every idea gets turned over before it's had time to feel like anything — tested, compared, held up against what it might become. Your attention isn't landing on what matters; it's spreading across everything that might, and the grip keeps tightening.

What all that gripping is for is enough satisfaction to feel ahead of time. Ahead there's a version where it finally pays off, so you push the care, and the pushing eats the thing you were looking after. Feel for the one pull that stays after an ordinary day. That pull isn't a calling to protect. It's an appetite you can feed.
cells.sheetLine: You grip the pulls so hard they can't grow.

cells.tense: You are standing at a door that is already behind you, still holding the handle.
cells.ask: Name one pull you've been calling unfinished and say what it's made of — a person, a craft, a place. Say it to one steady ear or write it on one sheet, no more.
cells.core:
You still recognise what matters. What stopped is the feeding. A pull shows up and before it can turn into anything, your attention swings away — onto the next errand, the noise, the practical thing in front of you. Nothing gets felt through, so nothing turns into satisfaction that would make the attention seem worth giving.

What's starved is the part that says this and not that. Not your ability to imagine; your willingness to say what one pull is made of. Start by saying it out loud. Name what the pull is made of and where it actually pulls. Once one other person has heard it, the attention tends to come back on its own.
cells.sheetLine: You know something is unfinished. You keep not saying what it's made of.

cells.tense: The pen is down in a room you are already writing, and you are asking whose book this is.
cells.ask: Set aside one stretch of ordinary time, pick one impression from it that wasn't aimed at you, and write what it was made of in two plain sentences.
cells.core:
You are already doing this — giving your attention to what matters in the lives around you, feeding some of it your time. But the credit gets sent elsewhere. You describe yourself as having no particular knowledge, just picking up what turns up. The picking runs; the owning doesn't.

What's missing is defining one thing by what it's made of and what it isn't. Sharpen one distinction and the whole pile gets clearer. What that costs to keep is honesty: put your cursor on one pull you've been calling ordinary and own that you chose to keep it around. That was your pick, whether or not you announced it.
cells.sheetLine: You're already tending what matters. You've not claimed it as yours.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the person's satisfaction or dissatisfaction depends on a process of feeling things through to the point where imagination settles — nothing in the record says their particular life works that way. A reader could reasonably say the real issue is time, money, or other people, not which pulls get attended to. The ask survives an incorrect read because naming what a pull is made of, or where it pulls toward, produces information whether or not that is the true problem, and none of the asks condition anything on the reading being right. The one sentence that serves me rather than them is 'Abundance felt rather than counted,' which is a good line and says nothing they can use.
